\chapter{Synthesis --- The Thing and the Person}
\label{ch:synthesis-two-sets}
\hlchaptermodality{97}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use both sets in one exchange and say what decides between them.}

Complete ES-C46-sintesis-dar-y-decir: run the four-turn exchange and say what separates lo from le.

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — the thing and the person, in one sentence}

\label{lesson:ES-C46-sintesis-dar-y-decir}



\begin{quote}
Two pronouns, one question. \emph{Lo} or \emph{le} — what decides?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Read this aloud and watch the two sets take turns.

\begin{quote}
— \emph{¿Tienes el libro?} — \emph{Sí, \textbf{lo} tengo.} — \emph{¿Y Ana?} — \emph{\textbf{Le} digo hoy.}
\end{quote}

Four turns. The book gets \emph{lo}, because the having lands on it. Ana gets \emph{le}, because the telling is aimed at her.

Nothing in the sentence shape tells you which. Same slot, two letters each, one Latin ancestor. \textbf{The only thing separating them is what you mean.}

That is new. Every choice so far could be settled by looking at something — a noun's ending, its article, where the stress falls. This one cannot.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: choosing at speed}]
In a real conversation you do not have time to run a test. So do not aim for the test — aim for the \textbf{feeling} of the two verbs:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Verbs that \textbf{hold, make, want, see} land on a thing. Those take \emph{lo}, \emph{la}, \emph{los}, \emph{las}.
  \item Verbs that \textbf{tell, speak, give, ask} are aimed at a person. Those take \emph{le}, \emph{les}.
\end{itemize}

Say enough sentences and the verb starts arriving with its pronoun attached, which is what fluency here actually is. The test is scaffolding for when you are unsure, not the method.

And when you get it wrong you will be understood: \emph{lo digo} and \emph{le digo} are both ordinary sentences. You will have said something slightly other than you meant, and the person will ask.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}lo tengo, le digo, los tengo, les hablo\textquotedblright{} until each verb brings its own pronoun
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{¿Tienes el libro?} (\emph{\textbf{Sí, lo tengo}}.) \textquotedblleft{}I tell her today\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{\textbf{Le digo hoy}}.) What decides between \emph{lo} and \emph{le}? (\textbf{What you mean} — nothing on the page.) Next: what happens when a sentence needs \textbf{both} at once.
\end{tcolorbox}
